board_asks: the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic and its two workhorses: HCF & LCM by prime factorisation (with HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers), and proving numbers like √2, √3, √5 irrational by contradiction. In the rationalised 2026-27 syllabus this chapter is short and mark-dense — prime-factorisation HCF/LCM and one irrationality proof carry almost every mark.

big_idea.tagline: Break every number into primes — the rest follows.
big_idea.body: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says every composite number is a product of primes in exactly one way (order aside). That single fact is the master key to this whole chapter: it gives you HCF and LCM by comparing prime powers, it explains why HCF × LCM = product of two numbers, and it powers the proofs that $\sqrt{2}$, $\sqrt{3}$ and $\sqrt{5}$ are irrational.

definitions.verbatim: Every composite number can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique, apart from the order in which the prime factors occur.
definitions.plain: Any composite number breaks into primes in exactly ONE way — only the order can differ. This uniqueness is what makes prime factorisation a reliable tool for HCF, LCM and irrationality proofs.

definitions.verbatim: Let p be a prime number. If p divides a², then p divides a, where a is a positive integer.
definitions.plain: If a prime divides $a^2$, it must already divide $a$ itself. This is the engine of every irrationality proof — it lets you conclude $2\mid a$ from $2\mid a^2$.

source.note: Theorem 1.2; superscript a² printed, linearised here

definitions.verbatim: a number 's' is called irrational if it cannot be written in the form p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0.
definitions.plain: A number you simply cannot write as one integer over another (with non-zero denominator). $\sqrt{2}$, $\sqrt{3}$, $\pi$ are irrational; every terminating or repeating decimal is NOT.

definitions.verbatim: The prime factorisation of a natural number is unique, except for the order of its factors.
Product of the smallest power of each common prime factor in the numbers.

concepts.title: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
concepts.body: Every composite number splits into primes in exactly one way (order aside). Build a factor tree — keep dividing by the smallest prime — until only primes remain, then collect them as powers, e.g. $32760 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 \times 13$.
concepts.tested: 1-2 mark 'express as a product of primes' / composite-number reasoning

concepts.title: HCF & LCM by prime factorisation
concepts.body: Prime-factorise each number. HCF = product of the smallest power of each COMMON prime; LCM = product of the greatest power of EVERY prime that appears. Line the powers up in a column and read them off.
concepts.tested: 2-3 mark 'find the HCF and LCM by prime factorisation'

concepts.title: HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers
concepts.body: For any two positive integers, $\text{HCF}(a,b) \times \text{LCM}(a,b) = a \times b$. So once you have the HCF you can get the LCM without re-factorising: $\text{LCM} = \dfrac{a \times b}{\text{HCF}}$. ⚑ Warning: this holds for TWO numbers only, never three.
concepts.tested: 1-2 mark 'given HCF, find LCM' (e.g. HCF(306,657)=9 → find LCM)

concepts.title: Proving irrationality by contradiction
concepts.body: To prove $\sqrt{p}$ irrational: assume it is rational, $\sqrt{p} = a/b$ with $a,b$ coprime. Square and rearrange to get $p \mid a^2$, so (by Theorem 1.2) $p \mid a$; substitute back to force $p \mid b$ too. Now $a$ and $b$ share the factor $p$ — contradicting 'coprime'. Hence $\sqrt{p}$ is irrational.

concepts.title: 'Can it end in 0/5?' — uniqueness in action
concepts.body: A number ends in 0 only if its prime factorisation contains BOTH 2 and 5. Since $4^n = 2^{2n}$ has no factor 5, it can never end in 0. The uniqueness half of the theorem is what lets you rule this out for every $n$ at once.
concepts.tested: 1-2 mark competency: 'check whether 6ⁿ (or 4ⁿ) can end with the digit 0'

examples.shape: HCF & LCM by prime factorisation · NCERT Example 2
examples.problem_verbatim: Find the LCM and HCF of 6 and 20 by the prime factorisation method.

solution_steps.lead: HCF = smallest power of each COMMON prime.
solution_steps.text: The only common prime is 2, smallest power $2^1$. So $\text{HCF}(6,20) = 2$.

solution_steps.lead: LCM = greatest power of EVERY prime.

examples.mark_logic: 2-mark shape: 1 for the two prime factorisations, ½ for the HCF (smallest common power) and ½ for the LCM (greatest powers of all primes).

examples.shape: HCF then LCM via HCF×LCM=product · NCERT Example 3
examples.problem_verbatim: Find the HCF of 96 and 404 by the prime factorisation method. Hence, find their LCM.

solution_steps.lead: HCF = smallest power of the common prime.
solution_steps.text: Only 2 is common; smallest power $2^2$. So $\text{HCF}(96,404) = 2^2 = 4$.

solution_steps.lead: Use HCF × LCM = product to get the LCM.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: 1 for the factorisations, 1 for HCF = 4, 1 for using HCF × LCM = product to get LCM = 9696 (the 'hence' signals you must NOT re-factorise).

source.note: problem on p.4; solution (LCM = 9696) completes on p.5

examples.shape: HCF & LCM of three numbers · NCERT Example 4
examples.problem_verbatim: Find the HCF and LCM of 6, 72 and 120, using the prime factorisation method.

solution_steps.lead: HCF = smallest power of each common prime.
solution_steps.text: $2^1$ and $3^1$ are the smallest powers of the common factors 2 and 3, so $\text{HCF}(6,72,120) = 2^1 \times 3^1 = 6$.

solution_steps.lead: LCM = greatest power of every prime.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: 1 for the three factorisations, 1 for HCF = 6, 1 for LCM = 360. Trap: for THREE numbers, HCF × LCM ≠ product — you must read the powers off directly.

examples.shape: Prove irrationality by contradiction · NCERT Example 5

solution_steps.text: Suppose $\sqrt{3}$ is rational: $\sqrt{3} = a/b$ with integers $a, b\ (b \neq 0)$ taken coprime.
$b\sqrt{3} = a \Rightarrow 3b^2 = a^2$, so $3 \mid a^2$, and by Theorem 1.2, $3 \mid a$. Write $a = 3c$.

solution_steps.lead: Force a shared factor, then contradict.
solution_steps.text: Substituting: $3b^2 = 9c^2 \Rightarrow b^2 = 3c^2$, so $3 \mid b$ too. Then 3 divides both $a$ and $b$ — contradicting coprimeness. Hence $\sqrt{3}$ is irrational.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: 1 for the coprime assumption, 1 for $3\mid a$ via Theorem 1.2, 1 for forcing $3\mid b$ and stating the contradiction. Skipping 'coprime' or the Theorem-1.2 justification loses marks.

source.note: √3 printed as a radical (Symbol-font glyph drops in extraction); prose + '3' skeleton verify

examples.shape: Rational ± irrational is irrational · NCERT Example 6

solution_steps.text: Suppose $5 - \sqrt{3}$ is rational: $5 - \sqrt{3} = a/b$ with coprime integers $a, b\ (b \neq 0)$.
The right side is a ratio of integers, so it is rational — making $\sqrt{3}$ rational. But $\sqrt{3}$ is irrational. So our assumption is wrong: $5 - \sqrt{3}$ is irrational.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: 1 for assuming rational, 1 for isolating $\sqrt{3} = (5b-a)/b$, 1 for the contradiction against $\sqrt{3}$ irrational. You must CITE that $\sqrt{3}$ is already proved irrational.

examples.problem_verbatim: Consider the numbers 4ⁿ, where n is a natural number. Check whether there is any value of n for which 4ⁿ ends with the digit zero.

solution_steps.text: A number ends in 0 only if it is divisible by 5 — i.e. 5 appears in its prime factorisation.
By the uniqueness of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic there is no other prime, so 5 never divides $4^n$. Hence there is NO natural number $n$ for which $4^n$ ends with 0.

examples.mark_logic: 2-mark competency shape: ½ for the 'must contain 5' condition, ½ for $4^n = 2^{2n}$, 1 for citing uniqueness to conclude no such $n$ exists. The same argument answers Exercise 1.1 Q5 ('can 6ⁿ end in 0?').

source.note: 4ⁿ printed with superscript n; skeleton normalises the superscript to 'n'

strategies.text: Prime-factorise, stack the powers in a column: HCF = smallest common power, LCM = greatest power of every prime.
Use $\text{LCM} = \dfrac{a \times b}{\text{HCF}}$ — don't re-factorise. (Two numbers ONLY.)
Assume $= a/b$ coprime → square → $p\mid a^2 \Rightarrow p\mid a$ (Theorem 1.2) → sub back → $p\mid b$ → contradiction.
Assume rational, isolate the surd = ratio of integers → 'rational surd' contradicts the known irrational.
Prime-factorise: ends in 0 needs BOTH 2 and 5; a sum with a common factor is composite.

pitfalls.text: Claiming HCF × LCM = product for THREE numbers. It holds for two numbers only.
Forgetting 'coprime' in an irrationality proof. The whole contradiction rests on assuming $a, b$ share no factor — skip it and the proof collapses.
Jumping from $p \mid a^2$ straight to $a = pc$ without citing Theorem 1.2. The step $p\mid a^2 \Rightarrow p\mid a$ is exactly what earns the mark.
Swapping the HCF/LCM rules — HCF takes the SMALLEST powers of COMMON primes; LCM takes the GREATEST powers of ALL primes.

third_tab_content.name: √2 is irrational — the proof by contradiction
third_tab_content.intro: This is NCERT's Theorem 1.3 (p.6-7). It is the model every irrationality proof in this chapter follows, and rests entirely on Theorem 1.2 ($p \mid a^2 \Rightarrow p \mid a$), which itself comes from the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. Learn this one and √3, √5 are the same argument with a different prime.

steps.claim: Assume, to the contrary, that √2 is rational.
steps.justification: Proof by contradiction: we suppose the negation and drive it to an impossibility.

steps.claim: Reduce to lowest terms, so the numerator and denominator are coprime.
steps.justification: Divide out any common factor to get a and b with no common factor other than 1.
From b√2 = a, squaring gives 2b² = a².
By Theorem 1.2, since the prime 2 divides a², it divides a. Write a = 2c.

steps.claim: Substitute back — now 2 divides b as well.
steps.justification: 2b² = 4c² gives b² = 2c², so 2 | b² and (again by Theorem 1.2) 2 | b.

steps.claim: Contradiction: a and b share the factor 2, yet we chose them coprime.
steps.justification: The contradiction arose from assuming √2 rational — so that assumption is false.

source.note: Theorem 1.3 statement + proof, pp.6-7; radicals are Symbol-font glyphs in the PDF
